content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studied the multi-task learning in offline setting. The authors proposed an uncertainty based algorithm inspired by the pessimism value iteration in single task offline setting. Empirically, the authors showed that their algorithm can outperform the baseline methods including CQL with Direct Sharing, CDS and CDS-Zero in most the evaluation tasks. They also provided some theoretical justification for their algorithms.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength

The idea of forming pessimism by subtracting uncertainty terms in sharing knowledge in offline multi-task setting seems somewhat new. The performance of their proposed algorithm seems outperform the baseline in most cases.

### Weakness

The main question I have is how the algorithm/theory analysis in this paper can handle the case when the multiple tasks are kind of different from the others, given that the authors did not have data selection step but instead transfer all of them. 

On the empirical side, I'm feeling if the other tasks are different from the current task, by directly using Eq. 8, the data from other tasks will significant bias the learned Q function from the true Q* in current task. I'm not sure if it is because the tasks are similar in the experiments part that this problem hasn't been observed in experiments. I would be appreciate it if the authors can explain more about it.

On the theory side, I'm feeling there are some mistakes when the authors adapting the theory from [3] to justify their methods and there are also some clarity issue in their proof. Different from [3] which considered single task learning in linear MDP, the authors in this paper considers multi-task learning, and it's unclear what assumptions they made about the similarity about the feature map $\phi_i$ and the linear transition kernel $P_i=\langle \phi_i, \mu_i \rangle$ between different tasks ($i$ is the task index here), especially the authors used the same feature map $\phi$ in this paper. 
Besides, in Page 18, the proof of Eq. (47), the authors directly refer [3] for detailed proof, while [3] only considers the single task setting. I do not understand why their proof can directly transfer here, and I feel there should be some bias term (maybe something captures the distance between tasks) occurs on the RHS.

As a summary, the method in this paper does not make sense to me and I would like the authors explain more details.


Besides, there are also some clarity issue:

(1) I do not understand Eq. (6) very well. According to Eq. (7), the term inside the expectation of Eq. (6) would just be the uncertainty term $\beta \Gamma$, which does not make sense. Or maybe you ``stop gradient'' of $\hat{\mathcal{T}}^{ood} Q_i$ during the training? But it is also weird since it always asks $Q_i$ to approximate something that is lower than itself, which will drag it to approach zero.

Besides, why it takes square after taking the expectation instead of before expectation?

(2) The author claims that $\hat{\mathcal{T}}^{UTDS} Q$ is a contraction mapping but just refer it to a book [1]. I would like the authors to clarify which chapter in [1] such result comes from, because intuitively speaking, when computing $\hat{\mathcal{T}}^{UTDS}$, it requires to subtract uncertainty term, which is different from the normal Bellman operator.

Besides, no matter whether it is a contraction operator, I would suggest the authors to make it clear what it converges to if applying $\hat{\mathcal{T}}^{UTDS}$ for multiple times (and whether it converges if it is not a contraction operator). I think it is important to justify the algorithm is doing something reasonable.

(3) The Sec. 4 is also hard to follow. I think the authors should first clarify that the linear MDP setting in [2-3] is episodic MDP (with finite horizon H), instead of the discounted MDP in this paper. This is crucial because in discounted setting Q/V function is stationary for all time step, while in episodic setting the Q/V function is usually time-dependent (since the horizon is finite). As a result, the authors should also specify the step index $h$ when they discussing the value function (and the uncertainty terms) in Sec. 4. Moreover, I think the authors should also discuss whether the gap/difference between discounted and episodic setting will weaken their explanation.

Besides, what is T in Thm. 2?


[1] Alekh Agarwal, Nan Jiang, Sham M. Kakade, and Wen Sun. Reinforcement learning: Theory and algorithms, 2022.

[2] Chi Jin, Zhuoran Yang, Zhaoran Wang, and Michael I Jordan. Provably efficient reinforcement learning with linear function approximation. In Conference on Learning Theory, pp. 2137–2143. PMLR, 2020.

[3] Ying Jin, Zhuoran Yang, and Zhaoran Wang. Is pessimism provably efficient for offline rl? In International Conference on Machine Learning, pp. 5084–5096. PMLR, 2021.

The algorithm has some novelty on the empirical side, while the theory in this paper is mainly adapted/extended from previous paper so the novelty on the theory side is limited.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1847 by Reviewer YJ56

content.title: Response to Reviewer YJ56
content.comment:
We appreciate the valuable review and suggestions. We have revised our work accordingly. In what follows, we address the concerns in detail.

**Comment 1.** On the empirical side, I'm feeling if the other tasks are different from the current task, by directly using Eq. 8, the data from other tasks will significant bias the learned Q function from the true Q* in current task. I'm not sure if it is because the tasks are similar in the experiments part that this problem hasn't been observed in experiments. I would be appreciate it if the authors can explain more about it.

**Response 1.** Thanks for the question. The effectiveness of algorithm is not due to the similarity among shared tasks. The most obvious evidence is the four tasks in the Jaco Arm domain, where the agents need to move the robot arm toward four different directions. As a result, the behavior policies among the four tasks differs significantly. According to the results given in Figure 3 (and also Figure 13, 16, and 19), policy constraint-based methods like CQL, CDS, and CDS-Zero all perform poor in data sharing. Since the distribution among different datasets behave very different, sharing data from other tasks introduces biases in the learning objective and exacerbates the distribution shift in policy constraints. 

In contrast, the proposed UTDS does not relies on the similarity between shared tasks. UTDS performs pessimistic learning based on uncertainty estimation rather than behavior cloning.  Intuitively, we measure the uncertainty of state-action pairs as $\Gamma^{\rm lcb}(s,a)=[\phi(s,a)^\top\Lambda^{-1}\phi(s,a)]^{\frac{1}{2}}$, which is the confidence interval of the value function. Consider an extreme case in tabular MDPs, where the state action feature $\phi(s,a)$ is a one-hot vector. Then we have $\Gamma^{\rm lcb}(s,a)=1/\sqrt{N(s,a)+\lambda}$, where $N(s,a)$ is the pseudo-count of the $(s,a)$ pair. In this case, even if we share data that are totally different from the main task, the optimality gap $\mathbb{E}_{\pi^*}[\Gamma^{\rm lcb}(s,a)]$ does not increase since the pseudo-count $N(s,a)$ cannot decrease with data sharing. As a result, even if data sharing does not benefit the data coverage of the optimal policy, it does not degrade performance. Such a key factor makes UTDS inherently different from the policy constraint methods that need appropriate data selection to select similar samples compared to the main task. We add more discussion in Appendix A in our revised paper.

**Comment 2.** Different from [3] which considered single task learning in linear MDP, the authors in this paper considers multi-task learning, and it's unclear what assumptions they made about the similarity about the feature map $\phi_i$ and the linear transition kernel $P_i=<\phi_i,\mu_i>$ between different tasks ($i$ is the task index here), especially the authors used the same feature map $\phi$ in this paper.

**Response 2.** Thanks for the question. We consider a multi-task data sharing settings defined as 
$\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,\gamma,{R_i,i}), $
where $i\in[1,m]$ and $m$ is the number of tasks from the same domain. In the same domain, all tasks share the same dynamics function, and the difference is the definition of reward functions. As a result, the offline datasets in the same domain have different behavior policies that optimize different cumulative rewards, while these tasks have the same dynamic function. The assumption of linear MDPs is defined as $P_t (s_{t+1} | s_t, a_t) = <\psi(s_{t+1}), \phi(s_t, a_t) >$, where the same $\psi$ and $\phi$ functions are used for all tasks in the same domain.

content.title: Response to Reviewer YJ56 (follow-up)
content.comment:
**Comment 3**. In Page 18, the proof of Eq. (47), the authors directly refer [3] for detailed proof, while [3] only considers the single task setting. I do not understand why their proof can directly transfer here.

**Response 3.** Thanks for your question. According to our analysis, the main difference between the single-task training and multi-task data sharing is the covariance matrix. (1) For training task $i$ with the single-task data $D_i$, the corresponding covariance matrix is 
$\widetilde\Lambda_i$. (2) For training task $i$ with the shared data $\widehat{D_i}=D_i \cup D_{j\rightarrow i}$, the new covariance matrix becomes $\widetilde\Lambda_{ij}=\widetilde\Lambda_i+\widetilde\Lambda_j$ (see Eq. (29)). We recall the main result in Corollary 1 is

$SubOpt(\pi_i^*, \widetilde\pi_i) \leq \sum_{t=1}^{T} \mathbb{E}_{\pi^*_i} [ \Gamma_i^{\rm lcb}(s_t,a_t;\widehat{D}_i)]$,  

$\leq \sum_{t=1}^{T} \mathbb{E}_{\pi^*_i} [ \Gamma_i^{\rm lcb}(s_t,a_t;\widehat{D}_i)]$

where the fist LCB-term is $[\phi(s_t,a_t)^\top\widetilde\Lambda_{ij}^{-1}\phi(s_t,a_t)]^{1/2}$, which uses the covariance matrix $\widetilde\Lambda_{ij}$ from the shared dataset, while the second LCB-term uses $\widetilde{\Lambda}_{i}$ as the covariance matrix.

The first inequality can be directly obtained from PEVI [1] since the covariance matrix $\widetilde\Lambda_{ij}$, learned policy $\widetilde{\pi}_i$ and the optimal policy $\pi_i^*$ are all defined in the shared dataset $\widehat{D}_i$. With uncertainty-based pessimism and reward relabeling, the suboptimality gap is determined by the data coverage of the optimal policy in the shared dataset. We revised Section 4 to add more details. 

*Reference*

[1] Jin Y, Yang Z, Wang Z. Is pessimism provably efficient for offline rl? ICML 2021

**Comment 4.** I feel there should be some bias term (maybe something captures the distance between tasks) occurs on the RHS of Eq.(47).

**Response 4.** We remark that the suboptimality gap of UTDS does not include a policy distance term between the main task and the shared task, which is the main difference between our method and policy constraint methods. In particular, for policy constraint methods, the suboptimality bound is closely related to the policy difference between shared tasks. As a result, sharing data across irrelevant tasks may exacerbate the distribution shift and hinder learning performance in policy constraint methods, as we discussed in Eq. (1) and Eq. (2). 

For our method based on uncertainty quantification, the optimality gap becomes tight if the data coverage of the optimal policy $\pi^*$ becomes better with data sharing, in the sense that the expected uncertainty under the optimal policy $\pi^*$ is smaller. According to Theorem 1 as $\Gamma_i(s,a;D_i) \geq \Gamma_i(s,a;\widehat{D}_i)$

since $\widetilde\Lambda_{ij} \succeq \widetilde\Lambda_{i}$, the suboptimality gap does not increase even we share datasets from totally irrelevant tasks. 

**Comment 5.** .. stop-gradient in $\hat{T}^{\rm ood}Q_i$ of Eq. (6) and Eq. (7)..., drag it to approach zero.

**Response 5.** We respectfully remind the reviewer that we have included a detailed analysis on this question in our manuscript after Eq.(7). We set ${\widehat{T}}^{\rm ood}Q_i(s,a^{\rm ood})$ as the learning target for OOD actions without gradient propagation.


To prevent this operator drag the Q-value to approach $-\infty$, we decrease $\beta_2$ exponentially with a factor $\alpha$ to prevent overly pessimism. Applying this operator for infinite times to $Q_i(s,a^{\rm ood})$ leads to $(\hat{T}^{\rm ood})^\infty Q_i(s,a^{\rm ood})$, which equals
\begin{equation}
Q_i(s,a^{\rm ood})- \sum\nolimits_{k=0}^{\infty} \alpha^k \beta_2\:\Gamma_i(s,a^{\rm ood})=Q_i(s,a^{\rm ood})-\frac{\beta_2}{(1-\alpha)}  \Gamma_i(s,a^{\rm ood}).
\end{equation}
Thus, iteratively applying the OOD operator does not lead to the negative infinity target. 

**Comment 6.** Besides, why it takes square after taking the expectation instead of before expectation?

**Response 6.** Thanks for pointing out this problem. We fix this typo in the revised manuscript.

**Comment 7**. $\widehat{T}^{\rm UTDS}Q(s,a)$ that is a contraction mapping with the uncertainty term.

**Response 7.** Thanks for the question. According to Lemma 1 in our manuscript, the uncertainty term is equivalent to $\Gamma^{\rm lcb}(s,a)$ in linear MDPs. The value of $\Gamma^{\rm lcb}(s,a)=[\phi(s,a)^\top\Lambda^{-1}\phi(s,a)]^{\frac{1}{2}}$ only relies on the state-action embedding in the offline datasets. Then we have the following lemma.

**Lemma** (contraction mapping) For state-action pairs from the offline dataset, the UTDS operator $\widehat{T}^{\rm UTDS}$ is a $\gamma$-contraction operator in the $\mathcal{L}_\infty$-norm.

content.title: Response to Reviewer YJ56 (follow-up)
content.comment:
We refert to Appendix A.5 for the proof. 
In addition, from the perspective of linear MDPs, UTDS aims to capture the epistemic uncertainty arising from solving a regression problem with the following target (or response), as $r_h(s_h, a_h) + \hat B_h Q_{h+1}(s_h, a_h)$, where $\hat B_h Q_{h+1}(s_h, a_h) = Q_{h+1}(s_{h+1}, a_{h+1})$ is the (empirical) transition operator, where $s_{h+1} \sim \mathbb{P}(\cdot|s_h, a_h)$ and $a_{h+1}$ is the greedy action. 

We add the penalty function $\Gamma_{h+1}$ into $Q_{h+1}$ and get $Q_{h+1}^-=Q_{h+1}-\Gamma_{h+1}$, yielding the pessimistic target as $r_h(s_h, a_h) + \hat B_h Q_{h+1}^-(s_h, a_h)$, where we assume that the reward function is known and deterministic for simplicity of discussion. 

The epistemic uncertainty in the above two equations arises from $\hat B_h$ rather than $Q_{h+1}$ or $Q_{h+1}^-$, which are treated as *fixed functions* when evaluating uncertainty, since they come from the $(h+1)$-th step. We emphasize the subscript $h+1$ to avoid confusion. We added the details in Appendix A.5.

**Comment 8.** The Sec. 4 is also hard to follow. I think the authors should first clarify that the linear MDP setting in [2-3] is episodic MDP (with finite horizon H), instead of the discounted MDP in this paper. ... the authors should also specify the step index when they discussing the value function (and the uncertainty terms) in Sec. 4...  discuss whether the gap/difference between discounted and episodic setting will weaken their explanation.

**Response 8.** Thanks for the question. We agree with you that the episodic setting in the theoretical analysis (without discounting) is different from the discounted setting in the practical algorithm. We use a discount setting (with $\gamma=0.99$) in our experiment for several empirical considerations. (1) Using $\gamma < 1$ is a standard setup in the implementation of deep RL algorithms to ensure empirical performances, even for episodic MDPs. For example, the value-based methods such as DQN (Mnih et al., 2015, Pages 6), bootstrapped DQN (Osband et al., 2016, Appendix D.2), IDS (Nikolov et al., 2019, Appendix A) all set $\gamma=0.99$. The policy-gradient methods such as DDPG (Lillicrap et al., 2016, section 7), TD3 (Fujimoto et al., 2018, Table 3), and PPO (Schulman et al., 2017, Appendix A) also set $\gamma=0.99$ in Mujoco tasks. (2) Although Deepmind Control Suite is an episodic task in our experiment, the episodic length is relatively long, typically with 1000 steps. Using $\gamma < 1$ ensures that the value functions are bounded, which improves the empirical performance of the algorithms.

To the best of my knowledge, there is currently less paper studying linear MDP in the discounted setting from the theoretical perspective. Meanwhile, it is hard to conduct experiments in episodic setting (In that case, the algorithm needs to learn the value function of all the possible horizon). Moreover, we can reduce an MDP with discounted rewards to episodic MDP by setting the effective horizon $H=1/\gamma$. This means that the theorem for episodic MDP can hold in the discounted setting. We added more discussions in Appendix B.3.

In our proof in the appendix, we omit the subscript of time step $h$ in the $Q$-function and the uncertainty since we have the subscript $i$ for the task id. Our discussion is applicable to the solution for arbitrary time step. 

**Comment 9**. What is T in Thm. 2

**Response 9.** Thanks for pointing out this problem. $\mathcal{T}V_{t+1}(s_t,a_t)$ is the true Bellman target based on the environment dynamics, as 
$$\mathcal{T}V_{t+1}(s_t,a_t):=r(s_t,a_t)+\gamma E_{s_{t+1}\sim P_t(\cdot|s_t,a_t)} \big[V_{t+1}(s_{t+1},a_{t+1})\big].$$

Theorem 2 shows that if we set $y = \mathcal{T} V_{t+1}(s^{\text{ood}}, a^{\text{ood}})$, then our estimation based on disagreement among ensembles is a valid $\xi$-uncertainty quantifier. However, such OOD target is impossible to obtain in practice as it requires knowing the transition at the OOD datapoint $(s^{\text{ood}}, a^{\text{ood}})$. In practice, if TD error is sufficiently minimized, then $Q_{t+1}(s, a)$ should well estimate the target $\mathcal{T} V_{t+1}$. Thus, in practice, we utilize 
\begin{equation*}
y = Q_{t+1}(s^{\text{ood}}, a^{\text{ood}}) - \Gamma_{t+1}(s^{\text{ood}}, a^{\text{ood}})
\end{equation*}
as the OOD target, where we introduce an additional penalization $\Gamma_{t+1}(s^{\text{ood}}, a^{\text{ood}})$ to enforce the pessimistic value estimation. We has revised Section 4 to add the details.

content.title: Thanks for the Reply
content.comment:
Thanks for the detailed reply by authors, which also addressed some of my concerns and made the setting more clear to me. Given that the authors considered the case where different tasks share the dynamics but have different reward function (seems also assumed the learner can query reward function for each task to relabel the data from other tasks), the methods and guarantee seems reasonable.

However, I still do not think this paper is enough for acceptance of ICLR. My main concern is that the assumptions that all tasks share the dynamic is quite strong, and over-simplified the problem setting, which makes the results in this paper very restrictive. Besides, under such an assumption, it's quite straightforward to consider using all the data from all the tasks since there is no difference on transition and also reward relabeling is available. Then, I don't see much novelty of the algorithm and results in this paper, because it seems there is no significant difference/additional challenges comparing with single task offline setting.

I would suggest the authors try to strengthen this paper by removing such an assumption (or at least allow small model difference), which I think would be more reasonable and interesting.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper applies a previously introduced Offline RL method to a mixture of datasets.
This datasets are obtained by applying policies that are optimised for different tasks within the same environment. 
The authors show that their benchmarked method does not rely on additional data selection to learn a policy for a specific task from these mixture datasets. 
This is possible because the penalty term of the method is based on uncertainty estimation instead of policy constraints.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths
- The theoretical analysis seems sound. 
  As usual for theoretical results in Deep RL papers, they seem quite disconnected from the experimental results, but the intuition they provide is reassuring and gives hope about the practical prowess of the algorithm.
- The proposed tasks and datasets are meaningful and align well with previous benchmarks in Offline RL.
  Furthermore, the new datasets are a good extension to these previous benchmarks.

### Weaknesses
- The proposed method appears to be merely an **application of PBRL** [(Bai et al., 2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.11566) to datasets in the Multi-Task Data Sharing (MTDS) setting.
  There is limited novelty in applying existing algorithms to new datasets.
- I do not see how relabelling with the **exact** reward function to obtain new datasets is any different from usual dataset mixing in standard Offline RL benchmarks.
- The results presented in Fig. 2 are not convincing. 
  It is possible to reduce epistemic uncertainty by adding more data.
  However, it is not guaranteed that this happens in relevant parts of the state-action space.
  Simply sharing a dataset might even have adverse effects locally. 
  This is actually exemplified in Fig. 2, as the upper left part has even higher uncertainty after sharing the dataset, wheras the other parts have lower uncertainty.
  Furthermore, typical state-action spaces are high-dimensional, which probably behaves differently than the two-dimensional example. 
  Maybe the authors could down-project (e.g. using a VAE as done for Fig. 1 in [(Smith et al., 2018)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.08533) ) the state-action spaces of some of the datasets in the experimental section for more convincing results?
- While the dataset creation and task selection are well considered, it is unclear how to evaluate a potential new algorithm under the proposed benchmark.
  It would be useful to have some sort of aggregate measure, e.g. the total return per *domain* given the proposed settings. 
  In general, it is hard to assess the benefit of UTDS/PBRL over its competitors from the qualitative results.

Minor Weaknesses: 
- The authors could be more clear about contributions, maybe by adding a list of contributions to the introduction.
- Fig. 2 lacks axis labels and axis captions. Fig. 3-6 lack the y-axis caption, even if it is obvious from the text. Same goes for Fig. 11-19.
- Fig. 3-6 (and 11-19) would benefit from indicating the return of the original dataset. 
  Then one can check if sharing other datasets helps to improve on the policy that created the dataset. 
  Otherwise one could just use Behavioral Cloning on the original dataset instead of running UTDS.
- The method named CDS-Zero (and Unlabeled-CDS on one occasion) was named CDS+UDS in the original publication. 
  This could cause confusion for future work and should be either renamed or stated to be dubbed CDS-Zero throughout the manuscript.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The theoretical analysis and experimental studies were conducted in a reasonable way. 
Furthermore, the provided code looks well structured, documented and simple to execute to reproduce the main findings.
Nevertheless, I don't think it is justified to present the proposed algorithm as a novel method.
After all, it is not simply inspired by, but rather an **application of the PBRL algorithm** [(Bai et al., 2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.11566). 
If the paper would have been framed as a benchmark, I would have been more inclined to give a positive assessment. 
An investigation of how the dataset distributions in the proposed benchmark differ from usual dataset settings in the [D4RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.07219) datasets (e.g. similar to [Schweighofer et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.04714)) could strengthen such findings, especially regarding the effect of mixing different datasets.
content.summary_of_the_review:
As iterated before, the proposed algorithm is practically an **application of PBRL** [(Bai et al., 2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.11566) and not merely inspired by it as claimed in the paper. 
I would argue that applying this algorithm to a specific selection of datasets is not novel enough to give a positive recommendation for this paper. 
Furthermore, there seem to be no fundamental differences between the MTDS setting and the usual Offline RL setting, if access to the true reward function is available for relabelling.
The main value of this manuscript lies in the introduced datasets from a general perspective of benchmarking algorithms for Offline RL.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1847 by Reviewer 8nDM

content.title: Response to Reviewer 8nDM
content.comment:
We appreciate the valuable review and suggestions. The major concern of the reviewer is the contributions of our paper. The reviewer think (1) the Multi-Task Data Sharing (MTDS) settings and (2) the proposed Uncertainty-based Data Sharing (UTDS) algorithm are not novel. In what follows, we address the concerns in detail. We have revised our work accordingly. 

**Comment 1.** I do not see how relabelling with the exact reward function to obtain new datasets is any different from usual dataset mixing in standard Offline RL benchmarks.

**Response 1.** Thanks for the question. We respectfully disagree about this statement for offline MTDS settings. To our knowledge, such a statement is only true for online RL setting. For offline RL, the datasets for various tasks are different in both the *behavior policies* and the *reward functions*. Relabelling the reward function eliminates the reward bias while the mixed dataset still contains different behavior policies. As a result, methods with explicit or implicit policy constraints will struggle in constraining the learned policy to different behavior policies. Especially, if the shared tasks are very different from the main task, the policy-constraint-based methods exacerbate the distribution shift and degrade the performance. As an example in our manuscript, the four tasks in Jaco Arm require moving the robot arm toward four different directions, which makes the behavior policies among tasks differ significantly. As shown in Fig. 3, directly sharing data with relabelled rewards performs poorly because of the exacerbation of distribution shift.

The motivation of this paper is closely related to the reviewer's comment, where we aim to propose an unified algorithm for both the single-task training and multi-task data sharing (without data selection). We show that purely uncertainty-based pessimism is suitable for MTDS in offline RL from both the empirical and theoretical perspectives. 

**Comment 2.** The proposed method appears to be merely an application of PBRL (Bai et al., 2022) to datasets in the MTDS setting. There is limited novelty in applying existing algorithms to new datasets.

**Response 2.** Thanks for the question. We highlight that the motivation of our manuscript is not to apply PBRL for MTDS settings, but to provide a unified algorithm for both the single-task and MTDS. Previous methods construct a shared dataset by selecting transitions with a conservative $Q$-value more than the top k-th quantiles. In contrast, our analysis show that a valid $\xi$-uncertainty quantifier is sufficient to achieve a unified view for single-task and MTDS. Our analysis in linear MDP shows that the optimality gap in MTDS is only related to the expected data coverage of the shared dataset on the optimal policy. Thus, UTDS is less affected by the change of behavior policy in data sharing. 

For implementation, instead of developing a purely new algorithm, we find that algorithms that use valid $\xi$-uncertainty quantification for pessimism meet such theoretical requirements. Offline RL methods based on ensemble uncertainties like PBRL [1], EDAC [2], and MSG [3] are all belong to such a category. In our paper, we extend PBRL for data sharing and provide theoretical and empirical analysis for this algorithm. 

*References*

[1] Pessimistic Bootstrapping for Uncertainty-Driven Offline Reinforcement Learning. ICLR 2022

[2] Uncertainty-Based Offline Reinforcement Learning with Diversified Q-Ensemble. NeurIPS 2021

[3] Why So Pessimistic? Estimating Uncertainties for Offline
RL through Ensembles, and Why Their Independence Matters. NeurIPS 2022

**Comment 3.** Fig. 2 is not convincing. ... Simply sharing a dataset might even have adverse effects locally. ... Furthermore, typical state-action spaces are high-dimensional... Maybe the authors could down-project ... the state-action spaces ... for more convincing results?

**Response 3.** 
Thanks for the question. The epistemic uncertainty refers to the uncertainty of the $Q$-function due to a lack of offline data. In linear MDP settings considered in our paper, the epistemic uncertainty is measured by 
$$\Gamma^{\rm lcb}(s,a)=[\phi(s,a)^\top\Lambda^{-1}\phi(s,a)]^{\frac{1}{2}},$$
where $\phi(s,a)$ is the feature map and $\Lambda = \sum^{|D|}_{k=1}\phi(s^k, a^k)\phi(s^k, a^k)^\top + \lambda I$ is the covariance matrix corresponding to the dataset. In Theorem 1 of our paper, we prove that for a given state-action pair $(s,a)$, the following inequality holds as 

$$\Gamma^{\rm lcb}(s,a;D_i)\geq \Gamma^{\rm lcb}(s,a;\widehat{D_i}),$$
where $D_i$ denotes the single-task dataset, and $\widehat D_i=D_i\cup D_{j\rightarrow i}$ denotes the shared dataset with relabelled data from task $D_j$. This inequality signifies that sharing data is *guaranteed* to reduce epistemic uncertainty in linear MDPs.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 8nDM (follow-up)
content.comment:
Consider an extreme case in tabular MDPs, where the state action feature $\phi(s,a)$ is a one-hot vector, then we have $\Gamma^{\rm lcb}(s,a)=1/\sqrt{N(s,a)+\lambda}$, where $N(s,a)$ is the count of the $(s,a)$ pair. Since $N(s,a)$ cannot decrease with data sharing, $\Gamma^{\rm lcb}(s,a)$ is also guaranteed to reduce with data sharing in tabular MDPs. We remark that in Figure 2, the uncertainty in the left part roughly unchanged after data sharing since the maximum uncertainty in left figure is large than the right figure. The corresponding uncertainty represented by the color map is normalized by the maximum and minimum uncertainty in each figure. 

Nevertheless, we agree with the reviewer that adverse effects can occur for several reasons. (1) The linear and tabular MDP settings assume that $\phi(s,a)$ is known and fixed in learning. In contrast, for DRL with high-dimensional states and actions, $\phi(s,a)$ is randomly initialized by a neural network and is often learned with the value function, which makes the uncertainty estimation inaccurate. (2) Since the calculation of the covariance matrix $\Lambda$ is computationally expensive with the changing $\phi(s,a)$, we use the ensemble $Q$-networks to estimate the uncertainty. Lemma 1 in Appendix A shows that the LCB-penalty and ensemble uncertainty are equivalent under mild conditions. In practice, the ensemble uncertainty is accurate with *infinite* networks, while it is unachievable and we only use *5* ensembles in our experiments. The empirical result shows 5 ensembles are sufficient to provide reliable uncertainty quantification and strong performance.  We follow the reviewer's suggestion and add a visualization of the uncertainty in offline data sharing in Appendix C.5. We share data from Walker Run task to Flip task, and Quadruped Roll-Fast task to Jump domain. The dimension reduction of the state-action pair is conducted by PCA. The result shows that the uncertainty around the main data slightly increases with data sharing, while it is sufficient to provide strong performance. 

**Comment 4**. While the dataset creation and task selection are well considered, it is unclear how to evaluate a potential new algorithm under the proposed benchmark. It would be useful to have some sort of aggregate measure ...

**Response 4**. Thanks for the suggestion. In our experiments, we use histogram for directly comparing the single-task and data sharing training scores. We add the results of aggregated score in the Appendix C.6 by following the reliable evaluation metrics proposed in [1], including median, mean, interquartile mean (IQM), and optimality gap. We refer to Appendix C.6 for the results.

[1] Agarwal R, Schwarzer M, Castro P S, et al. Deep reinforcement learning at the edge of the statistical precipice. NeurIPS, 2021

**Comment 5**. The authors could be more clear about contributions, maybe by adding a list of contributions to the introduction.

**Response 5**. Thanks for the question. We include a summary of our contribution in the revised paper.

**Comment 6**. Fig. 2 lacks axis labels and axis captions. Fig. 3-6 lack the y-axis caption, even if it is obvious from the text. Same goes for Fig. 11-19.

**Response 6.** Thanks for pointing out this issue. We have fixed this problem in the revised paper.

**Comment 7.** Fig. 3-6 (and 11-19) would benefit from indicating the return of the original dataset. Then one can check if sharing other datasets helps to improve on the policy that created the dataset. Otherwise one could just use Behavioral Cloning on the original dataset instead of running UTDS.

**Response 7.** Thanks for the question. We add the score of behavior policy in Figure 8, 9, 10 and Table 3 in Appendix C.1. The result shows UTDS trained in single-task dataset outperforms behavior policy on average. We also remark the score of behavior policy often outperforms behavior cloning (BC) since BC will imitate both the good actions and bad actions in a mixed dataset. In our experiments, we consider that direct sharing with CQL is a kind of behavior cloning algorithm since CQL contains a policy constraint term as $\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\frac{\pi(a|s)}{\pi_b(a|s)}-1]$ according to Theorem 3.5 in the CQL paper.  

**Comment 8.** The method named CDS-Zero (and Unlabeled-CDS on one occasion) was named CDS+UDS in the original publication. This could cause confusion for future work and should be either renamed or stated to be dubbed CDS-Zero throughout the manuscript.

**Response 8.** Thanks for pointing out this problem. Since the name UDS (i.e., Unlabeled Data Sharing) [1] is very similar to our algorithm's name UTDS (i.e., Uncertainty-Based Data Sharing), we revise our manuscript and use CDS-Zero to avoid confusion.

[1] Yu T, Kumar A, Chebotar Y, et al. How to Leverage Unlabeled Data in Offline Reinforcement Learning. ICML 2022

content.title: Response to Reviewer 8nDM (follow-up)
content.comment:
**Comment 9.** If the paper would have been framed as a benchmark, I would have been more inclined to give a positive assessment. An investigation of how the dataset distributions in the proposed benchmark differ from usual dataset settings in the D4RL datasets (e.g. similar to Schweighofer et al., 2022) could strengthen such findings, especially regarding the effect of mixing different datasets.

**Response 9** Thank you for praising our contribution in the datasets and benchmark. To our knowledge, we release the first multi-task offline dataset in the community, which contains 12 popular continuous control tasks from 3 domains. We collect 5 types of datasets for each task. Meanwhile, we release a benchmark to evaluate the state-of-the-art algorithm in single-task and multi-task data sharing in our datasets. We will try to give more analysis about the datasets.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on offline reinforcement learning with Multi-Task Data Sharing (MTDS), specifically in scenarios where the dataset for a specific task is limited. However, existing methods are inefficient in calculating the policy constraints and abandon a large portion of datasets. This paper proposes an uncertainty-based MTDS approach that shares the entire dataset without data selection. The authors further provide theoretical analysis, which shows that the optimality gap of our method is only related to the expected data coverage of the shared dataset, thus resolving the distribution shift issue in data sharing.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The idea of this paper is straightforward and make sense. Figure 2 is a very good example to illustrate the uncertainty quantification of UTDS.
2. This paper provides a theoretical analysis, which shows that the optimality gap of the proposed method is only related to the expected data coverage of the shared dataset.
3.  The experimental results show the proposed algorithm outperforms the previous state-of-the-art methods in challenging MTDS problems.


Weaknesses:

1. Lack of ablation study. It is better to add the ablation study of the penalty of OOD loss and the number of ensembles.
2. Since the proposed method considers an ensemble way to estimate uncertainty, it is better to compare the training and inference time with baselines.
3. How to sample OOD action and OOD state? This part is not clear.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is well-presented and organized. The proposed idea is a simple combination of PBRL (or EDAC) and MTDS. The authors provide an excellent code for experiment result reproduction.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper is well-presented and organized. Even the idea the simple and straightforward. The empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. However, I have several concerns about this paper:
1. Since the proposed method is a combination of existing work, an ablation study is necessary to identify the contribution of each component. Otherwise, it is difficult to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
2. As the proposed model consider the ensemble method in the algorithm, it is better to discuss the time complexity and compare the running time in the training and inference stages.
3. How to sample OOD action and OOD state in Section 3.2?
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper focuses on offline reinforcement learning for multi-task. The authors consider policy learning for multiple tasks, with a small fixed dataset corresponding to each task. The proposed method UTDS is based the multi-task data sharing, i.e. relabelling transitions from other tasks with the reward function of the target task. Given the mixed dataset with transitions shared from other tasks, this paper proposes to train an ensemble of Q functions to measure the uncertainty of value estimation for state-action pairs, and perform pessimistic value iteration. Additionally, the proposed method penalizes the value of out-of-distribution actions with uncertainty quantification.

This paper provides a theoretical analysis that the optimality gap of the proposed method is only related to the data coverage of the shared datasets. Experiments are conducted on locomotion tasks on Walker, Quadruped, and manipulation tasks on Jaco Arm. The proposed method shows advantages over the baselines given different datasets with different qualities.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
This paper studies an interesting and important problem in offline RL, i.e. sharing and making full use of transitions across multiple tasks.
The proposed method UDTS is relatively simple and avoids wasting data on other tasks to some extent.
The authors provide theoretical and empirical results to demonstrate the advantage of UDTS.

Weaknesses:
The novelty may not be very strong, because the method is to apply existing uncertainty-based offline RL algorithms (EDAC or PBRL) to multi-task sharing datasets (correct me if I misunderstand). And the dataset sharing via reward relabelling is not novel, either.
The evaluation and comparison with baselines can be improved. Logically, any offline RL algorithm on a single task can be applied to multi-task sharing datasets. So the baseline called direct sharing can incorporate stronger offline RL algorithms, especially the ones without policy constraints (see more details below).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
The paper is generally clearly-written. Especially Figure 1 and 2 are informative to help readers' understanding.
The description in Sec. 3.2 may need further revision for clarification. "Eq. (5) only captures the uncertainty of experiences from the in-distribution data". But in Eq. (5), the uncertainty term \Tau_i(s',a') takes a'\sim \pi_i as input and this a' may not be in-distribution data. "We sample OOD actions following the learned policy". Why do actions following the learned policy definitely belong to the out-of-distribution set?

Quality:
The evaluation can be improved.

As for the baseline of direct sharing, is it possible to compare the proposed method with more recent state-of-the-art offline RL algorithms, such as IQL and trajectory transformer on the multi-tasks shared dataset, instead of only CQL? Also, could you apply EDAC and PBRL directly on the multi-task sharing datasets, and report their performance? If the proposed method can beat these prior works, the advantages of UTDS are more convincing. 

It will be great to see an ablation study about the two components in Eq (8). I'm curious about the importance of L_{ood}(s) in Q function learning.

Ablation study about hyper-parameter \beta_1, \beta_2 and \alpha will be very helpful. Is UTDS sensitive to the value of these parameters? Is there any intuitive explanation about the role of these hyper-parameters and how to tune them given new datasets?

Can the proposed method be extended to other multi-task settings? For example, in MetaWorld, the tasks are to operate different objects. So the multiple tasks not only differ in reward functions but also differ in dynamics when the robot hand manipulates different objects. Can we share datasets across tasks in this setting, so that at least the transitions of the moving robot hand itself can be utilized across tasks?

Novelty:
The novelty of the method itself is a bit unclear. Is UTDS equivalent to PBRL on multi-task sharing datasets? If not, what's the subtle difference between UTDS and PBRL? The theoretical analysis is relatively novel.

Reproducibility:
The reproducibility is good in that the code and datasets are shared.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper introduced an approach for multi-task offline RL with theoretical and empirical results. But the novelty should be clarified more and the evaluation part can be improved.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
